items.title: Effects of land acknowledgements on non-Indigenous audiences in Australia and the USA
items.author: Kyle Peyton
items.content: McNamee and Peyton find that land acknowledgements raise awareness of, but not curiosity about, Indigenous nations. These practices improve organizational reputations, but their effects on political attitudes and support for reparations are insignificant.

items.title: Why girls have worse mental health than boys
items.content: Analyses of data from more than 3,000 adolescents found that loneliness and desire for thinness contribute to the higher prevalence of depressive symptoms and suicidal ideation among girls than in boys. Young people’s perspectives informed the pathways that were investigated.

items.title: Understanding the structural and psychological bases of inequality
items.content: Inequalities in education, health, technology and social status are often studied in isolation. This Focus issue shows how these inequalities are interconnected in the real world, and how competing views of fairness shape the responses to them. To reduce inequality, we need more research on the drivers: how complex interactions among individual beliefs, institutions, technologies and environments widen the gaps or create opportunities for change.

items.title: There is no clear target for replication rates
items.author: Mark Rubin
items.content: Is a 50% replication rate too high, too low or just right? We need a target replication rate to answer this question. Here, I evaluate two potential target rates, the ‘optimal’ replication rate and the ‘expected’ replication rate, and I call for an educational intervention to better appreciate their limitations.

items.title: Meritocracy and inequality acceptance
items.author: Bertil Tungodden
items.content: The idea of meritocracy — that income differences should reflect performance rather than luck or inherited privilege — can be used to justify inequality. Yet people who consider meritocracy to be fair may disagree about redistribution. Understanding these disagreements can help to reduce polarization.

items.title: What chimpanzees at war have taught me about being human
items.author: John C. Mitani
items.content: Seeing a deadly ‘civil war’ unfold among chimpanzees has been a painful experience for John Mitani. His decades of watching wild great apes now evoke his family’s experience with xenophobia. But to him, the war highlights what makes humans unique: not our conflicts, but our unparalleled capacity for tolerance and cooperation.
